wrong: Ends the output with print and expects it to appear right away. | right: Finish a line of print calls with println; some systems hold print output until a newline is printed.
wrong: Ends the output with print and expects it to appear right away. | right: Finish a line of print calls with println; some systems hold print output until a newline is printed.

[0] everyday_reading (E): Everyday meaning: 'print' means send to a printer, and an output command lists each distinct name once. Java rule: System.out.print(x) displays x's characters in the terminal at the current position, with no newline, every time it runs.
[1] misconception (M) -> RepeatedOutputVariablePrintedOnce: wrong rule: An output statement that names the same variable twice prints it only once. Right rule: Each expression in the output is printed, so a repeated variable prints its value each time.
[2] inconsistent_trace (T) -> RepeatedOutputVariablePrintedOnce: Applies the print rule (LT) unevenly: inserts a line break after a print on one line but not another, or drops a repeated value. (here mixing in: "An output statement that names the same variable twice (WRITE y, x, y) prints it only once")
[3] misconception (M) -> ParenthesesOnlyIfArgument: wrong rule: () are optional on a call with no argument. Right rule: A method call always needs parentheses after the name.

[0] names_the_element (N): System.out.print(x) is a library method call (on the PrintStream System.out) that displays x in the terminal without ending the line.
[1] states_the_rule (S): print(String s) prints the string (or "null" for a null reference); print(int) etc. print the value's string form; no line terminator is written.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): The argument expression is evaluated first, converted to a string, then its characters are written at the current output position; the next output continues right after them.
[1] output_prediction (OP): Output is exactly the characters of the value (a string literal without its quotes, a number in decimal) and nothing else: print("Goodbye, "); println("cruel world"); prints Goodbye, cruel world on one line.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): One call appends the value's characters to the output and leaves the cursor on the same line; it changes no variable and returns nothing (void).

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): System.out.print(s); is a statement, so its output appears at its place in the statement sequence.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): print("s") outputs exactly the characters between the quotes, without the quotes; spaces inside the quotes are printed.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): print leaves the cursor on the same line; println ends the line; a line built from several prints should end with println.
[3] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Purpose: build one line of output from several pieces (a prompt, labels and values) before ending it with println.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> RepeatedOutputVariablePrintedOnce: Changing print to println (or back) moves the following output to a new line (or the same line) but keeps the characters printed; swapping two print statements swaps their text.
[1] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Finish a line of print calls with println. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: the last output of the program is a print: on some systems the text is held and not shown, or the prompt appears on the same line
[2] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Use print when more output must follow on the same line (prompts, items in a row); use println to end a line, and printf when the number format matters.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A method call needs parentheses and correct case. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: System.out.print "x"; or System.out.Print(x)

print leaves the cursor on the same line after printing; println moves the cursor to the next line after printing.
System.out.print(s); is itself a statement, so it runs at its own place in the sequence of statements.
print("s") outputs exactly the characters between the quotes, without the quotes.
